div.p: THE CENTRAL GESTURE IN JASPERS' PHILOSOPHY
JEANNE HERSCH

It is, I think, a constant characteristic of any deep philosophical system that you can recognize, in any of the work of its author, the same scheme of thought, the same spiritual “gesture”, whatever the topic he is in the process of dealing with. The reader may often get an impression of monotony, as if it could not have been “written in any other way”, as if he could have guessed in advance what he has just read for the first time. Such an experience has much to do with the Platonic “reminiscence”. On the other hand less profound thinkers tend to be far more unpredictable and each time invent with much ingenuity new solutions to new problems they are dealing with.

Karl Jaspers belongs to the first category. You can open any of his books anywhere and you will recognize “the sound of his thought” at once, whatever the topic may be. At the end of this talk I shall try to explain why, in philosophy, depth and monotony belong together.

The first move of Jaspers’ thought is oriented towards reality as that which is given in front of him, in an attempt to catch Being as a totality and a unity. But he fails. Any search for serious knowledge begins with dissociating “the world” into a plurality of aspects, of perspectives, which it is impossible to sum up in a unity, and which are also discontinuous due to the specific mode of each one of them. The evidence of any specific knowledge on one level depends in each case on the specific viewpoint and on the methods adopted — so that every particular knowledge is always relative to the definition of this aspect, of this viewpoint, of this method — it is never an absolute knowledge of the world as such. The world as a unity and a whole remains out of reach.

The first move is, then, an attempt which fails, not because of a mistake, but because it must fail. This failure is a creative one; it has the effect of throwing the subject back on to himself, as he is the point of departure of the attempt and of its failure as well.

What am I, as a subject which is confronted with “the world”? Here again, the subject would like to grasp itself as the being it is, as a unity. But it must recognize in itself, as a subject in the world and towards the world, the plurality and discontinuity of its own viewpoints and intentions.

The subject is alive, and as such it has needs and wants, it is threatened by death, it has vital interests for which it must fight. As such, it is also concretely located in space and time, under certain circumstances
which it did not choose, but upon which its life is dependent. This is what Jaspers calls Dasein.

But when the subject tries to acquire a knowledge of the world, what it aspires to is not this practical, vital knowledge any more. It wants to get a knowledge independent of its situation and interests, an apodictic knowledge, valid for everyone, justified by rationality and empirical verification. In this kind of research, it does not act as Dasein anymore, but as what Jaspers calls “Bewusstsein überhaupt”, that is to say “consciousness in general”, which is impersonal, common to any human subject as such, in so far as it wants to acquire objective knowledge.

And that is not enough. As a subject, I want to interpret the world with the help of great unities and meanings. I am not alone. I belong to a culture which tends to impose its schemes, demands, values. I don’t have to accept them as they are, I can change and correct them for good reasons, but I cannot do without them. That means that as a subject towards the world, I am not only Dasein, not only consciousness in general, but also, as Jaspers says (using here in a somewhat polemical way an expression of Hegel’s) “Geist”, “spirit”, aiming at global meanings and unities.

The subject fails, it cannot reach its own unity. As you can see, the first gesture of Karl Jaspers towards unity and totality fails, not only on the side of the world, but also on the side of the subject, of the self. But for Jaspers, the experience of failure at a limit which cannot be transgressed is always a creative experience. The limit itself is not like a dead wall, but it has a “beyond” which, through our failure, affects us. On the side of the subject, this “beyond” is what Jaspers calls “Existence”, and on the other side, the side of what the subject is not, is what he calls “Transcendence”, or often also “God”.

For Jaspers, “Existence” means, roughly speaking, authentic freedom, it is the emergence of a free decision, hic et nunc, in which the self commits itself absolutely. It is not something which could be grasped or stated like a fact or phenomenon, and therefore Jaspers speaks mostly when he is not “living existentially” but only speaking or writing about Existence, of “possible Existence”. It means that, in theory, Existence is only a possibility. It is real in the actual decision. The failure in the theoretical attempts to reach being as a unity in the world or in the subject is in itself a call for Existence to actualize itself “beyond” any objectivity or subjectivity (in a psychological sense). Jaspers says: “Es appelliert an Existenz”.

Now it would be wrong to think that Existence, awakened by the failure against the limit of empirical reality, is not in the world of space and time any more. On the contrary: an existential decision is always precisely connected with a concrete given situation. It cannot be generalized. It is only valid hic et nunc. That means that the failure is not the source of any new extended knowledge or of any quasi magic apprehension of the whole which could not be reached before. By no

means: Existence is in time. But it does somehow cross time (Jaspers says: quer zur Zeit), as in time everything is relative and interdependent whereas Existence is like the eruption in time of the absolute of beyond.

It means that, located in time, Existence can only be as related to this “beyond”. It always stands in the presence of Transcendence, knowing that it has not created itself, but that it is to itself a gift of Transcendence. Indeed, Existence has not created itself, nor can it be derived from anything else but Transcendence. For Jaspers, these two notions are correlated and neither of them has any meaning without the other.

As I said, Transcendence is sometimes called God. But it cannot be known, as God is claimed to be known in specific institutionalized churches, thanks to a Revelation or a Book. Transcendence is not a compensation for the failure of the quest of total and unified knowledge. It is a presence, but in no way a possession. On the contrary: if it is God, it is the hidden God — deus absconditus.

Let us try now to understand — or imitate — the central gesture of Jaspers. It is, first, an attempt to reach the totality and unity of being as world or as self. This is an extremely demanding and critical attempt, so demanding and so critical that it leads to the experience of its impossibility: every science is engaged in a search without end; every science is relative to its specific viewpoint and methods, so that altogether the sciences do not constitute a science of the whole. They are objective sciences. Even if they try to achieve a knowledge of the subject, it will be of the subject without its subjectivity — and there is no knowledge which could encompass the subject and the object; that is to say, which could reach being.

Instead of achieving a unified and total knowledge of being, the thinker experiences the failure of this knowledge — together with a call for an absolute presence — Existence in front of Transcendence.

The central gesture of Jaspers is a search for knowledge up to the limits which cannot be transgressed, the experience of failure at these limits and, because of this failure, the arising of a call for absolute presence, hic et nunc, of Existence in front of Transcendence.

In all the works of Jaspers, it seems to me, we find, in very different ways, this same gesture. There is a move towards a whole, which, in the human condition, cannot be grasped, and a transcending move which, without ever leaving the human reality, requires an absolute response. It is as if the essence of philosophising were to engage oneself into an “in-between”, beyond any possible knowledge of empirical reality, and before any possible freedom, giving itself up in a mystical unity.

Such a scheme is not without similarity, for instance, with the Platonic method of dialogue, with its constant move between the level of empirical things and the one of Ideas. The chief difference is, maybe, that for Plato the lowest level is the one of everyday practical action, and the highest the one of contemplation, whereas Jaspers “philosophising” each time consists in substituting for the failing theoretical knowledge a decisive,
present act of Existence. There is a greater similarity to Kant, where “pure reason”, theory is only freeing space, but the steps towards Transcendence are steps of “practical reason”, of freedom.

Let me give a few instances where we will be able to recognize the same central gesture of Jaspers’ thought. In psychiatry: Jaspers requires the utmost careful exploration of possible physiological factors of the disease as well as of the objective physiological facts. But the more careful and complete the picture of these elements is, the more it becomes evident to the psychiatrist that the medical “explanation” (“erklärende Psychologie”) is not sufficient, however necessary, and should not be the only approach. Jaspers listens very carefully to what the patient himself has to say about his subjective experience and he tries “to understand” it in a way completely different from that used in the causal explanations mentioned before. The “understanding psychology” (“verstehende Psychologie”) is not a method by which the causes of the disease are established, but one through which the process described and experienced by the patient, is subjectively “imitated” by oneself. When you say to a friend, “I understand you”, it does not mean that you know the causes of his behaviour, but that you can put yourself in his skin and go subjectively through the same development.

Now, Jaspers shows that neither the “explaining psychology” nor the “understanding psychology” is able to reach a knowledge of any mental disease as a whole: each of these methods, and both together, can only approach different aspects of it, aspects of the sick self. Yet both should remain clearly distinct from each other, so that a plurality of distinct methods is required, none of which has the right to be elusive of the others, as if it could reach the whole. This was the chief criticism Jaspers directed against psychoanalysis: it has a pretense to exclusiveness, taking advantage of a methodical lack of clarity, pretending to be “explanatory” whereas the meaning of the terms it used actually required a subjective “understanding”. We recognize here, in the field of psychiatry, the plurality of approaches, aiming at an unreachable whole, the experience of a necessary failure, and the existential meaning of this failure, which reveals the irreducible self of the patient — beyond all methodical approaches — as a possibility of Existence in its authenticity. Jaspers used to say that even in the worst mental disease an ultimate possibility of Existence cannot be denied and requires absolute respect.

A quite different example: Jaspers’ conception of existential “communication”. This communication could perhaps be less important in times when human beings have a common creed, live in a common order and enjoy common purpose of life. But communication becomes an existential need in a broken world, where traditional values are less and less effective. When the common symbols and sense of transcendence have lost their power, the self of the thinking individual becomes empty, looks upon an empty everyday life which is no real life at all. Frightening

questions then arise: “Who am I? What am I here for?” The social duties and tasks are no answer. It is necessary, but not enough, to find the way to one’s own solitary responsibility and freedom. The self is looking for a truth which it cannot reach by itself, but only in a communication with another self, a truth in which both are at the same time absolutely rooted, each in terms of its own human translation of Transcendence, and totally ready to recognize the translation of the other.

That means that neither can pretend to possess truth as such, no one is in possession of irrefutable arguments, to force the other to submission, as if it were possible for him to possess a direct and objective knowledge of Transcendence or a perfectly univocal Word of God. Here we see again: the non-possession of the transcendent truth, together with the certainty of Transcendence, is what makes true communication possible, as an endless search for meaning of the “inexhaustible ciphers”.

There is not only the failure to possess Transcendence in communication; communication itself is never completely realised. Each self is too narrow, or too possessive, or yields too easily to convenience. In communication, the two are not and should not be one. There is always guilt in this never ending and never won “loving fight”. But here the failure has once again a most precious result: thanks to this experience of failure, human beings deepen their sense for a truth which is beyond any particular knowledge, never possessed, and the condition for existential loving communication.

A last example: on the level of faith. For Jaspers there is more than a distinction, there is an opposition between the religious faith of somebody who belongs to a religious institution and recognizes the authority of certain persons or writings and what Jaspers calls “philosophical faith”. There is, as I have often observed, a constant misunderstanding about this question. The objections of Jaspers are by no means of an agnostic nature, they do not belong to the thinking of the “Aufklärung”. This can be shown with great evidence if we consider the discussion which took place between him and Bultmann, the protestant theologian. Paradoxically, the theologian recommended a modern “translation” of the Holy Scriptures, so as to make them acceptable for minds shaped by modern, scientific and objective thought, whereas the philosopher wanted to keep them in their literal authenticity. We must try to explain why: the reason is once again that it is necessary to go through a failure of the understanding if one wants to reach the transcendent meaning. It would be an error to change the religious language of the Holy Scriptures, which can be deciphered as a “Chiffreschrift” by a reader existentially engaged in front of Transcendence, to change it into a modern rationalised language giving the misleading illusion of an adequate, literal knowledge.
It is only through the experienced failure of directly expressing God in a human language that we become able to grasp the true meaning of
transcendent message, which remains always “in suspense” (“in der Schwebe”).

The mind, reaching the human limits of knowledge and of thought through rigorous methods, experiences, in the limitations and relativity of what can be achieved, the human finitude; and at the same time the meaning of this limitation and relativity, for Existence as an absolute commitment.

Existence fails in finding its origin in itself, or in the world. Its origin is in transcendence. It fails in any attempt to obtain anonymous, general knowledge: it only has convictions. It does not make statements, but takes absolute decisions. It is the origin of the real meaning of scientific knowledge as a mode of truth — but it fails to reduce this knowledge, or the knowledge of the self, to this kind of knowledge.

Philosophy is a human matter, without firm evidence, without support from any authority and without power. It is neither rationalist nor antirationalist: it uses rationality to reach the limits of it. Its chief instrument is failure, and it teaches the good use of failure. If there is a “negative theology”, Jaspers offers us a “negative philosophy” which is in his eyes the only honest way today to reach through the negation what is beyond nihilism. Jaspers wrote:

Philosophy in principle recognizes all phenomena as relevant to it only insofar as they can serve as symbols of the prior actuality of transcendence. In its search, it grasps symbols as possible vestigia dei, not God itself in his secrecy (Vernunft und Existenz, Wolters, Groningen, 1935).
